title: More Challenges To Church-State Wall Coming To Schools
author: Peter Greene
summary: Six months after the Supreme Court blocked Oklahoma's St. Isidore Catholic charter, Peter Deutsch filed a letter of intent for a Ben Gamla Jewish charter school in Oklahoma. The proposed school pairs Oklahoma academic standards with Jewish religious studies, mirroring St. Isidore. Approval is not the target; denial is. Denial gives Becket (the unbeaten religious liberty law firm) a federal challenge on the same grounds as St. Isidore but with a Jewish plaintiff, complicating political read and creating a cleaner test case. Local Jewish leaders were blindsided; the proposal is litigation-first. Ben Gamla is operationally run by Academica, a for-profit charter management company providing facilities, finance, staffing, and compliance. The archival value: the church-state question in public charters is not settled post-St. Isidore but a live pipeline of test cases built by an organized legal operation positioned to run federal sequences.
points: A second sectarian charter proposal in Oklahoma appears designed to generate a federal challenge with a different religious plaintiff, not to win local approval.
Becket law firm has undefeated Supreme Court record and is strategically positioned to escalate denial to federal court.
Local community leaders (including Jewish leaders) were not consulted and express that the school is not needed, suggesting the purpose is litigation-driven.
For-profit charter management company Academica operates the schools' operations and compliance, obscuring sectarian elements behind corporate structure.
quotes: In May of this year, the Supreme Court ended the hope that an Oklahoma Catholic charter school would be first in the nation to shatter the wall between religion and public schools. Now two schools are poised to challenge the notion that a public charter school must be non-sectarian.

On November 3, Peter Deutsch submitted a letter of intent to apply for charter authorization to the Oklahoma Statewide Charter School Board (the same board that previously approved St. Isidore), as reported by Nuria Martinez-Keel at Oklahoma Voice.

Deutsch, a representative of the National Ben Gamla Jewish Charter School Foundation, previously founded a chain of Ben Gamla non-religious Hebrew-English charter schools in Florida. The proposed school would be their first school outside of Florida.
Local Jewish leaders say they were blindsided by the proposal and argue that such a school is not needed. But approval does not appear to be the real goal here.

Eric Baxter, vice-president and general counsel at Becket, a leading religious-liberty law firm that is representing Ben Gamla, said we would represent Ben Gamla challenging that decision in the federal courts in Oklahoma. Becket boasts an unparalleled, undefeated record at the Supreme Court.

Ben Gamla schools are actually run by Academica, a Florida for-profit charter management organization that provides facilities, finance, staffing and human resource coordination, as well as bookkeeping, budgeting, regulatory compliance and financial forecasting.

According to the letter of intent, the proposed school would provide Oklahoma's state-approved academic standards alongside Jewish religious studies, enabling students to achieve college readiness while developing deep Jewish knowledge, faith, and values within a supportive learning community.

As Ben Gamla is proposing almost exactly what St. Isidore offered, it seems very likely that the Oklahoma supreme court would rule against them, thereby setting up a federal challenge.” Archived from Curmudgucation (Substack, originally Forbes.com) on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
